title: High-Fructose Corn Syrup vs Sugar: Are They Really Different?

seo.title: High-Fructose Corn Syrup vs Sugar
seo.meta_description: Common HFCS contains about 42% or 55% fructose, while sucrose is 50% fructose and 50% glucose joined together. Once digested, the common forms deliver broadly similar mixtures of fructose and glucose.
seo.search_intent: Compare high-fructose corn syrup with table sugar in composition, calories, metabolism, and practical nutrition.

excerpt: HFCS and table sugar are chemically different sweeteners, but the common HFCS-42 and HFCS-55 formulations have fructose-to-glucose proportions close to sucrose. The useful nutrition message is to limit total added sugars rather than treat one as uniquely harmless.
content_html:
The name “high-fructose corn syrup” sounds as if it must contain far more fructose than table sugar. In the common U.S. formulations, the difference is much smaller: HFCS is usually about 42% or 55% fructose, while sucrose is exactly 50% fructose and 50% glucose.

The sugars are arranged differently

Sucrose is one molecule made from glucose and fructose chemically bonded together. In HFCS, glucose and fructose are already present as free sugars in water. Digestion rapidly splits sucrose into its two components, so both sweeteners ultimately deliver glucose and fructose.

The common proportions overlap closely

HFCS-42 is used in many baked and processed foods; HFCS-55 is common in soft drinks. Their fructose proportions bracket the 50% found in sucrose. Both provide roughly 4 calories per gram of carbohydrate.

FDA does not identify common HFCS as uniquely unsafe

FDA says it is not aware of evidence showing a safety difference between foods containing HFCS-42 or HFCS-55 and foods containing similar amounts of traditional nutritive sweeteners with comparable glucose and fructose content.

The bigger question is how much added sugar the food contains

A beverage with 40 grams of added sugar remains a high-added-sugar beverage whether the sweetener is sucrose or HFCS. Use Added Sugars on the Nutrition Facts label to judge quantity instead of relying on the sweetener name alone.

faq.question: Is HFCS pure fructose?
faq.answer: No. Common HFCS contains both fructose and glucose; the most common forms are about 42% or 55% fructose.

faq.question: Is table sugar 50% fructose?
faq.answer: Yes. Sucrose contains one glucose and one fructose unit, a 50:50 ratio by molecule.

faq.question: Is HFCS more dangerous than sugar?
faq.answer: FDA says it is not aware of evidence showing a safety difference between common HFCS and similar amounts of other nutritive sweeteners with comparable glucose-fructose composition.
